items.body: An agent learns by interacting with an environment. At each step it observes a state, chooses an action, receives a reward and moves to a new state. Example: a robot learns a route by receiving rewards for reaching its destination and penalties for collisions.

items.title: Linear regression cost function and why
items.body: The usual cost is mean squared error: MSE = (1/n) sum(y_i - predicted_y_i)^2. Squaring prevents positive and negative residuals from cancelling and penalizes large errors. For ordinary linear regression, the objective is convex in the coefficients, which supports straightforward optimization. It also corresponds to maximum likelihood under independent Gaussian errors with constant variance.
items.final: Usually MSE; it is smooth and convex for ordinary linear regression.

items.title: Sigmoid, ReLU and preference for ReLU
items.body: Sigmoid(z) = 1/(1+exp(-z)), with output between 0 and 1. ReLU(z) = max(0,z). Sigmoid saturates for large positive or negative inputs, so its derivative approaches zero. For positive inputs, ReLU has derivative 1, helping gradients propagate and making computation simple. ReLU can still produce dead neurons for persistently negative inputs. Sigmoid remains appropriate for binary classification output probabilities.
items.final: ReLU is usually preferred in hidden layers; sigmoid is useful at binary output.

items.title: TF-IDF and word relevance
items.body: Term frequency measures how often a term occurs in a document, often normalized. Inverse document frequency downweights terms appearing in many documents: a simple form is idf(t)=log(N/df(t)); practical variants use smoothing. TF-IDF = tf(t,d) x idf(t). A frequent word in one document that is rare across the corpus receives a large weight. A ubiquitous word receives a small weight. Example: in a corpus of 100 documents, a term in only 2 documents has idf=log(50).
items.final: High local frequency plus low corpus frequency gives high TF-IDF.

items.body: Symmetric/private-key encryption uses the same secret key for encryption and decryption, is efficient for large data, and requires secure secret distribution. items.title: Design and verify an RSA e-certificate system
items.body: Setup: SUST creates an RSA signing key pair in protected storage and distributes an authenticated verification key through a trusted certificate chain. Issuance: form a canonical credential containing student identity, degree, issuer, unique serial and issue date; hash and sign it using a standard RSA signature scheme such as RSA-PSS. Holder: the student stores the document with its signature. Verification: the authority obtains the trusted issuer key, checks validity and revocation status, recomputes the credential hash and verifies the signature. A changed credential fails verification. In the textbook abstraction, s=m^d mod n and s^e mod n=m follows from the RSA exponent relation; real RSA-PSS verifies an encoded hash, not raw document exponentiation.

items.title: Unsalted hashes and salting complexity
items.body: Without salts, equal passwords yield equal hashes and one precomputed dictionary can be compared with many accounts. Suppose there are U accounts, D guesses and cost C per hash. An attacker can compute D hashes, roughly D*C work, and look up matches across all unsalted accounts. Unique salts prevent reuse across accounts; attacking all accounts with D guesses each requires roughly U*D*C work. Attacking one chosen account still costs roughly D*C. A salt is stored openly and does not increase the password’s inherent entropy. Combine unique salts with a costly password-hashing scheme.

items.body: Virtual memory gives each process an address-space abstraction, isolation, protection and the ability to use more address space than physical RAM. The OS maps virtual pages to physical frames using page tables; the MMU translates addresses, and a TLB caches translations. Demand paging loads pages when needed. Good replacement policies, locality and sufficient memory limit expensive page faults. Virtual memory is not inherently faster than direct RAM access; TLBs and locality reduce its overhead.
items.final: Page tables map addresses; TLBs accelerate translation; paging must avoid excessive faults.

items.title: TCP session hijacking
items.body: At a conceptual level, an attacker attempts to impersonate a participant in an established TCP connection by obtaining enough session/sequence context to make injected traffic appear valid, or by compromising an endpoint or traffic path. TCP alone does not authenticate application data cryptographically. Authenticated TLS, secure endpoint handling, unpredictable initial sequence values and network anti-spoofing reduce risk; TLS is the core application-data defense.
items.final: Hijacking forges participation in an existing connection; authenticated encryption protects its data.

items.body: A botnet is a collection of compromised devices remotely coordinated by an operator. items.title: How a TLS certificate helps against fake websites
items.body: During a correctly validated TLS handshake, the browser checks the certificate’s hostname, validity and chain to a trusted authority, and the server proves possession of the corresponding private key. An attacker serving a fake site at an unauthorized endpoint cannot normally impersonate the genuine hostname without satisfying these checks. The authenticated handshake establishes protected session traffic. A certificate identifies a domain/key binding; it does not certify that all business content is trustworthy.

items.title: Why usability matters
items.body: Usability lets specified users achieve goals effectively, efficiently and with satisfaction in a specified context. It reduces errors, training effort and frustration, improving task completion and accessibility. Example: a clear course-registration flow helps students submit the right courses without repeated help.

items.title: Universal Design principles
items.body: The seven commonly taught Universal Design principles are equitable use; flexibility in use; simple and intuitive use; perceptible information; tolerance for error; low physical effort; and size and space for approach and use. Example: a campus kiosk offers readable text, audio alternatives, reachable controls and confirmation before destructive actions. These are distinct from Nielsen’s usability heuristics.

items.body: It is a design heuristic claiming users should reach desired information within three clicks. items.title: Low- and high-fidelity café app prototypes
items.body: A prototype is a representation used to explore and test a design before committing to a full implementation. Low fidelity: paper sketches of menu, cart, checkout and pickup; ask users to order while a facilitator switches screens. It is cheap, quick and good for comparing flows. items.body: The common guidance is that users should quickly understand a page’s purpose and value; after roughly ten seconds without engagement or useful feedback, attention may drift. items.title: Hypotheses and keyboard experiment variables
items.body: A hypothesis is a testable statement about a population or effect. H0 usually expresses no difference/effect; H1 expresses a difference, or a specified direction if defined in advance. Control variables might include text length/difficulty, instructions and environment. Counterbalance order to limit learning/fatigue. items.title: Project manager’s role in planning and scope
items.body: The manager coordinates stakeholders to clarify goals, requirements, exclusions and acceptance criteria; creates or coordinates the scope baseline and WBS; estimates resources, cost and schedule; assigns responsibilities; and establishes risk, communication and change-control plans. Example: for a portal, agree that registration is included but hostel allocation is deferred, then assess any request to add it against time and cost.
items.final: Align expectations, establish the plan and control scope changes.

items.title: Proactive versus reactive risk strategies
items.body: Proactive management identifies and analyzes possible problems before they occur and implements preventive measures, such as load-testing before registration day. Reactive management responds after a problem occurs, such as restoring service after an outage. Prepared contingency responses are planned proactively but executed when triggered. Good management combines prevention with recovery readiness.
items.final: Proactive reduces risks beforehand; reactive addresses their realized consequences.

items.title: Software versus traditional project management
items.body: Both manage scope, time, cost, people, quality and risk. Software adds distinctive challenges: intangible deliverables, high requirements volatility, complex integration, difficult progress visibility, knowledge-intensive work and cheap replication after development. Iterative delivery and automated tests can give early feedback. Avoid claiming traditional projects never change or never use iterative methods; the differences are matters of degree and domain.
items.final: Shared management foundations, with greater software-specific uncertainty and intangible progress.

items.title: Major causes of software project failure
items.body: Common contributors include unclear goals, unstable/uncontrolled scope, unrealistic estimates, weak stakeholder engagement, poor communication, missing skills/resources, architectural/integration problems, inadequate testing and unmanaged risk. These reinforce one another: rushed planning creates an impossible schedule, which encourages skipped checks and rework. Define failure against agreed goals rather than assuming delay is the only criterion.
items.final: Requirements, planning, communication, engineering quality and risk failures often interact.

items.title: Four risk-response strategies for the data-loss scenario
items.body: Avoid: remove the risky activity, for example do not store unnecessary sensitive customer data. Reduce/mitigate: use reliable storage to lower likelihood, and tested daily backups to lower impact; these are two dimensions of the same response category. Transfer/share: buy cyber-insurance for specified financial consequences; it does not remove technical responsibility. Accept: knowingly tolerate small residual corruption risks with monitoring and a defined response. The question asks for four strategies, but its explicit reliability and backup examples both represent reduction. The avoidance example is added to complete the standard four-strategy set.
items.final: Avoid, reduce, transfer and accept; reliability and backups both belong to reduction.

items.title: Sample 4-mark question: assess whether a review pilot worked
items.body:
Question: A team pilots peer review on one module and sees fewer escaped defects. What evidence is needed before extending the change across the organization? Explain how to avoid a misleading improvement claim.
Answer: Define the baseline, measurement period and escaped-defect rate relative to comparable size or usage. Check whether the module, team experience, release size or test effort changed at the same time. Record review effort and cycle time as well as defects, so improvement in one metric does not hide excessive cost. Replicate or extend the pilot cautiously, collect team feedback and decide whether to standardize or revise the change. Use a repeatable improvement cycle and preserve the evidence.
items.final: Compare normalized baseline and pilot outcomes, inspect confounds and repeat before standardizing.

items.title: Sample 4-mark question: choose process measures
items.body:
Question: A company reports 100% compliance with its new development checklist, yet customer defects keep rising. Propose four measures that could reveal whether its process improvement is useful.
Answer: Track escaped defects per release or unit of delivered functionality; track lead time from approved work to release; track change failure/recovery outcomes; and collect user-reported task problems or satisfaction for the changed product. Define each consistently and compare over a suitable period. Inspect changes in release complexity and reporting behavior. Checklist compliance is an activity measure, while these outcomes test whether the process achieves its goals.
items.final: Measure quality, delivery flow, release reliability and user outcomes, not compliance alone.

items.title: Sample 4-mark question: align improvement frameworks
items.body:
Question: Two teams use different improvement frameworks and want to share lessons without forcing identical workflows. Design a lightweight coordination approach.
Answer: Agree common business outcomes and a small measurement vocabulary while allowing each team to tailor its workflow. Share an improvement backlog, pilot hypotheses, baseline/results and lessons in periodic reviews. Map comparable practices across frameworks rather than equating certification labels. Adopt only changes supported by evidence and revisit them when context changes. This combines shared learning with local adaptation.
items.final: Share outcomes, evidence and learning while tailoring team practices.

items.title: Sample 4-mark question: repair overlapping work packages
items.body:
Question: An online booking project assigns both the payment team and notification team responsibility for sending payment receipts. How would you repair the WBS and acceptance criteria?
Answer: Identify one accountable work-package owner for the receipt capability and document the interface: payment publishes a confirmed-payment event; notification consumes it and sends the receipt. Define behavior for duplicates, failures and retries, with explicit tests and ownership. Remove duplicate scope/cost entries, ensure every necessary activity still belongs somewhere and update the WBS dictionary and estimates. Dependency timing belongs in the schedule.
items.final: Clarify boundaries, ownership and interfaces; remove double-counted scope.

Question: A library-booking project receives a request for screen-reader support shortly before release. What planning evidence should be examined before agreeing a revised delivery commitment?

items.title: Sample 2-mark question: compare COCOMO size revisions
items.body:
Question: With unchanged Basic COCOMO mode coefficients, an estimate grows from 20 KLOC to 30 KLOC. Express the effort ratio without choosing numerical coefficients.
Answer: E1=a*20^b and E2=a*30^b. Divide to cancel a: E2/E1=(30/20)^b=1.5^b. Thus the effect depends on the size exponent; it is not necessarily a 50% effort increase.
items.final: Effort ratio = 1.5^b.

items.title: Sample 2-mark question: sensitivity and estimation confidence
items.body:
Question: Why should a manager present a COCOMO estimate as a range when requirements and size are uncertain? State two reasons.
Answer: First, effort depends on uncertain size, so plausible size bounds produce different effort outputs and can be amplified by the exponent. Second, calibration assumptions about the project/team may be imperfect, so one precise-looking output can hide model error. Present scenarios and update them as evidence improves.
items.final: Size uncertainty and model/calibration uncertainty justify a range.

items.title: Decision trees for risk evaluation
items.body: Represent a choice as a decision node and its uncertain outcomes as chance branches. Assign probabilities and monetary outcomes, including relevant costs. Calculate EMV = sum(p_i × outcome_i) at each chance node and work backward to choose the preferable option. Example: a risky option gives +100,000 with probability 0.6 and −40,000 with probability 0.4, so EMV = 60,000 −16,000 = 44,000. A certain +35,000 has lower EMV, but a risk-averse decision maker may still prefer it. EMV is not a guaranteed outcome.
items.final: Compare probability-weighted outcomes by rolling back a decision tree.

items.title: Waterfall drawbacks and the spiral model
items.body:
Waterfall proceeds through requirements, design, implementation, testing and delivery. Its weaknesses include expensive late changes, late user feedback and integration/testing problems discovered after substantial work. It suits stable, well-understood requirements better than highly uncertain ones.
The spiral model repeats a risk-driven cycle: establish objectives, alternatives and constraints; evaluate alternatives and resolve major risks, often through prototypes; develop and verify the next product level; review results and plan the next cycle.
Merits: early attention to high risks, repeated stakeholder feedback, incremental commitment and accommodation of change. Demerits: risk analysis needs expertise, management overhead can be high, completion can be difficult to bound and it may be excessive for small low-risk work.
items.final: Waterfall handles change poorly; spiral uses repeated risk-driven cycles.

items.title: Stages of contract placement
items.body: 1. Analyse requirements and define the required deliverables, quality and acceptance criteria. 2. Prepare an invitation to tender or request for proposals with scope, deadlines and evaluation criteria. 3. Identify suitable suppliers, issue the invitation and manage clarifications fairly. 4. Evaluate proposals using the stated technical, commercial, capability and risk criteria; shortlist and check evidence, demonstrations or references. 5. Negotiate scope, responsibilities, acceptance, payment, intellectual property and change procedures. 6. Award and sign the contract, notify bidders appropriately and hand it to contract management for monitoring. Placement ends with the agreement; ongoing supplier monitoring follows it.
items.final: Requirements → invitation → supplier proposals → evaluation → negotiation → award.

items.title: Hackman–Oldham job characteristics model
items.body:
The paper’s “Oldhun-Hackman” refers to Hackman and Oldham. Five core job dimensions are skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback. The first three support experienced meaningfulness; autonomy supports responsibility; feedback gives knowledge of results. These psychological states can promote intrinsic motivation, satisfaction and effective work, moderated by individual and contextual differences.
Motivating Potential Score: MPS=[(skill variety + task identity + task significance)/3] × autonomy × feedback, using compatible rating scales. Example: give a developer ownership of a complete user-facing feature, freedom over implementation within constraints, and direct feedback about how it works.
The supplied Week 11 page does not explicitly cover this model. Supplemental primary reference: Hackman & Oldham, Motivation through the design of work: test of a theory (1976), DOI 10.1016/0030-5073(76)90016-7.
items.final: Five dimensions support meaningfulness, responsibility and knowledge of results.

items.title: Fixed-price contract: advantages and disadvantages
items.body:
The supplier agrees a price for a defined scope, subject to the agreed change terms. Customer advantages: greater initial budget predictability, easier bid comparison and more cost-overrun risk allocated to the supplier. Supplier advantages: clear commercial target and potential gain from efficiency.
Disadvantages: a precise scope is needed; uncertainty may produce a large risk premium; changes require negotiation and can trigger disputes; a supplier under pressure may cut corners unless quality and acceptance are explicit. The supplier bears estimation/overrun risk. A fixed price does not mean every later scope change is free.
items.final: Budget clarity and efficiency incentives, but scope rigidity, risk premiums and change disputes.

items.title: Risk assessment and formula
items.body: Risk assessment identifies and analyzes uncertain events to prioritize response. A quantitative expected-loss measure is risk exposure RE=P(event) × loss if it occurs. Example: probability 0.2 and loss 50,000 gives RE=10,000 in expected monetary loss. For a probability-impact matrix, ordinal category scores can be multiplied for prioritization, but the result is a ranking score rather than a literal currency expectation. Also inspect high-impact risks that a simple average can obscure.
items.final: Risk exposure = probability × consequence (expected loss when quantified).

items.title: Leadership models and leader functions
items.body:
Style models distinguish autocratic/directive decisions, democratic/participative decisions and laissez-faire/delegated working. Their suitability depends on urgency, competence and coordination needs; delegation still requires accountability.

Leader functions include setting direction, organizing responsibilities, communicating priorities, motivating and developing people, resolving conflict, removing obstacles, representing the team and monitoring outcomes. Use the printed question table, not a similar textbook table: Project 1 year 3 is 20,000, and Project 3 year 5 is 20,000. All values use the table’s unstated currency unit.
Step 1: net profit = total positive inflows − initial investment. Step 2: compute cumulative cash flow until investment is recovered. Step 3: use the course’s annual ROI/ARR = (net profit / 5) / initial investment × 100%.
Project 1: inflows=160,000; net profit=160,000−100,000=60,000. Cumulative at years 0–5: -100,000, -90,000, -80,000, -60,000, -40,000, 60,000. Payback=4+40,000/100,000=4.4000 years. Average annual profit=60,000/5=12,000; ROI=12,000/100,000×100=12.00%.
Project 2: inflows=1,150,000; net profit=1,150,000−1,000,000=150,000. Cumulative at years 0–5: -1,000,000, -800,000, -600,000, -400,000, -200,000, 150,000. Payback=4+200,000/350,000=4.5714 years. Average annual profit=150,000/5=30,000; ROI=30,000/1,000,000×100=3.00%.
Project 3: inflows=130,000; net profit=130,000−100,000=30,000. Cumulative at years 0–5: -100,000, -70,000, -40,000, -10,000, 10,000, 30,000. Payback=3+10,000/20,000=3.5000 years. Average annual profit=30,000/5=6,000; ROI=6,000/100,000×100=6.00%.

items.title: Perceptron limitation and logistic regression
items.body:
A single perceptron learns a linear separating boundary and is guaranteed to converge only when data are linearly separable under the usual assumptions. With overlapping classes it can keep changing weights without finding a perfect separator; its hard step output is not a calibrated probability.
Logistic regression uses p(y=1|x)=sigmoid(w·x+b), a smooth cross-entropy objective and probabilistic outputs. It can fit a best-compromise linear classifier to overlapping data with regularization. Important correction: ordinary logistic regression still has a linear decision boundary in its input features; it does not by itself solve XOR or arbitrary nonlinear separation. Use nonlinear features, kernels or multilayer models when needed.
items.final: Logistic regression gives smooth probabilistic fitting; both ordinary models have linear boundaries.

items.title: Dimensionality reduction and PCA compression
items.body:
Reducing dimensions can reduce storage/computation, remove redundant directions, improve visualization and sometimes reduce noise/overfitting. It may also discard predictive information.
PCA steps: split data; fit training means and scale features if their units require it; center the training matrix X; obtain principal directions from its covariance eigendecomposition or SVD; sort by decreasing variance; retain k directions. Compressed representation Z=X_centered W_k. Reconstruction X_hat=Z W_k^T+mean. When k<original dimension, reconstruction loses variation in discarded directions. Choose k using explained variance and task validation, and reuse the training transformation on test data. PCA maximizes retained variance, not class separation.
items.final: PCA projects centered data onto k high-variance orthogonal directions.

items.title: TF-IDF and word relevance
items.body: Term frequency measures how often a term occurs in a document, often normalized. Inverse document frequency downweights terms appearing in many documents: a simple form is idf(t)=log(N/df(t)); practical variants use smoothing. TF-IDF = tf(t,d) x idf(t). A frequent word in one document that is rare across the corpus receives a large weight. A ubiquitous word receives a small weight. Example: in a corpus of 100 documents, a term in only 2 documents has idf=log(50).
items.final: High local frequency plus low corpus frequency gives high TF-IDF.

items.title: Find the most discriminative feature
items.body:
A discriminative feature helps distinguish target classes. On training data, compare each feature’s association with the class using an appropriate measure: information gain for categorical splits, or a justified statistical score for numerical inputs. Validate usefulness using a model and held-out or cross-validated permutation importance.
For information gain: compute parent class entropy, partition by a feature, calculate weighted child entropy and subtract it. Larger gain means greater impurity reduction for that split. Use identical evaluation conditions for all candidates and avoid test-set leakage. Correlated features and high-cardinality splits can mislead simple rankings; no dataset is supplied here, so no particular feature can be named.
items.final: Compare label-separation scores and validate predictive contribution without test leakage.

items.title: SVM slack variables and nonlinear separation
items.body:
For labels y_i∈{−1,+1}, soft-margin SVM minimizes (1/2)||w||²+C sum ξ_i subject to y_i(w·φ(x_i)+b)≥1−ξ_i and ξ_i≥0. ξ=0 meets the margin; 0<ξ<1 is inside it but correctly classified; ξ>1 is on the wrong side (ξ=1 lies at the decision boundary).
Slack permits overlap or noisy points at a penalty; large C penalizes violations more strongly. Slack alone does not create a nonlinear boundary. A nonlinear feature map φ, typically computed through a kernel, supplies nonlinear separation in the original input space.

items.title: Spam confusion matrix and all metrics
items.body:
Take Spam as positive. True positives: rows 2,4,8 → TP=3. False negatives: rows 1,9 → FN=2. False positive: row 5 → FP=1. True negatives: rows 3,6,7,10 → TN=4.

items.title: Batch gradient descent versus SGD
items.body: Batch gradient descent computes one gradient using the entire training set before updating weights: θ←θ−η∇J_all(θ). It gives a stable full-data direction but each update may be expensive. items.title: Why k-NN is nonparametric and how ties are resolved

items.title: Possible attack on one-time-pad encryption
items.body:
A correctly used OTP with a uniformly random secret key as long as the message, used exactly once, has perfect secrecy against ciphertext-only recovery. There is no generic brute-force method that uniquely identifies the true plaintext without additional information.
A reused pad is vulnerable: C1 xor C2=P1 xor P2 exposes relations between messages. OTP also lacks integrity: a ciphertext bit flip causes the corresponding plaintext bit flip, so known-format messages can be modified without learning the key. Key theft or nonrandom pads break the assumptions.
items.final: Correct OTP resists plaintext recovery, but pad reuse, key compromise and unauthenticated modification are threats.

items.title: Why a switch is usually safer than a hub
items.body: A hub repeats incoming signals to other ports, so any attached device can observe traffic on that shared segment. A switch learns MAC locations and normally forwards known unicast frames only to the relevant port, reducing casual interception. items.title: Second-preimage versus collision resistance
items.body: Second-preimage resistance: given one particular message m, it should be infeasible to find a different m′ with H(m′)=H(m). Collision resistance: it should be infeasible to find any distinct pair m,m′ with equal hashes; neither is fixed in advance. For an ideal n-bit hash, generic work is about 2^n for second preimages and 2^(n/2) for collisions, subject to the usual idealized assumptions.

items.title: Ten security principles
items.body:
1. Economy of mechanism: keep the trusted design small and understandable. 2. Fail-safe defaults: deny access unless it is explicitly granted. 3. Complete mediation: check authorization for every relevant access. 4. Open design: rely on protected keys, not secrecy of the design. 5. Separation of privilege: require independent conditions for sensitive access.
6. Least privilege: grant only the permissions needed. 7. Least common mechanism: minimize shared mechanisms that can leak or couple users. 8. Psychological acceptability: make secure use understandable and practical. 9. Work factor: ensure bypass costs are sufficiently high relative to attacker resources. 10. Compromise recording: make successful or attempted misuse detectable and attributable through protected audit records.
This is the classic eight design principles plus the two additional considerations often taught with them; the paper itself does not enumerate its intended list.

items.title: Buffer overflow and conceptual stack layout
items.body:
A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes beyond a buffer’s allocated bounds. In a vulnerable stack frame, an unchecked write may corrupt adjacent local variables, control data or a saved return address. items.title: Birthday paradox and hash collisions
items.body:
Assume independent, uniformly distributed birthdays over 365 days and ignore leap days. For 58 people, no collision requires each new birthday to differ from all earlier ones: P(no match)=(365/365)(364/365)…(308/365). Therefore P(at least one match)=1−product(i=0..57)(1−i/365)=0.99166498, or 99.1665%. This supports the paper’s approximately 99% statement; it is not exactly 99%.
For an ideal hash with N equally likely outputs and q independent distinct-message hashes, P(collision)=1−product(i=0..q−1)(1−i/N). When q is small relative to N, this is approximately 1−exp(−q(q−1)/(2N)). About 50% collision probability occurs near q≈sqrt(2N ln 2)=1.1774 sqrt(N). Thus an n-bit hash has generic collision-search scale 2^(n/2), rather than 2^n. Real nonuniform birthday patterns and nonideal hash functions need separate analysis.
items.final: 58 uniform birthdays give about 99.12% match probability; generic n-bit hash collisions take order 2^(n/2) trials.

Given p=59, generator g=2, Bob’s private exponent x=25 and message M=8. Compute y=g^x mod p=2^25 mod59=11. Public parameters are (p,g,y)=(59,2,11); if the question calls it a public-key pair, (g,y) is the pair with modulus p understood.

Bob computes s′=c1^x modp=16^25 mod59=9. Its inverse modulo59 is 46, since 9×46≡1. Recover M=c2×(s′)^−1 mod59=13×46 mod59=8.

items.title: Salted-password search space
items.body:
A 2-byte salt has 2^16=65,536 possible values. A dictionary of 1,000,000 candidate words combined with every possible salt gives 1,000,000×65,536=65,536,000,000 word–salt combinations. This is the all-salt precomputation space under the question’s apparent interpretation.
Important distinction: a normal stored salt is public. For one chosen account with its salt already known, the attacker needs only the 1,000,000 dictionary guesses, each hashed using that known salt. Salting prevents reusable precomputation across salts; it does not add secret-password entropy.

Multiple hosts reply to the victim, producing reflection and possible amplification. The diagram shows the mechanism rather than an operational attack procedure.

Defend by disabling IP-directed broadcasts, blocking inappropriate broadcast echo responses, filtering spoofed source addresses and monitoring/rate-limiting abusive traffic. Reflection depends on vulnerable network behavior; it is not a feature every modern network permits.

items.title: Adware and spyware with flow diagrams
items.body:
Adware displays advertising and may be bundled with other software; its behavior ranges from consented advertising support to unwanted or deceptive conduct. Spyware covertly monitors and collects activity or sensitive data without appropriate consent. The two can overlap when advertising software secretly tracks people.
The diagram contrasts advertising display with covert collection/transmission. Reduce risk through trusted installation sources, meaningful consent, restricted permissions, endpoint protection and removal of unwanted applications.
items.final: Adware serves advertising; spyware covertly collects information.

items.title: Establishing a client–server SSL/TLS connection
items.body:
The question uses SSL terminology; obsolete SSL is not appropriate for deployment. A conceptual modern TLS 1.3 handshake is: client sends ClientHello with supported parameters and key share; server selects parameters and returns ServerHello/key share; the server supplies its certificate and proof of key possession plus Finished; the client validates identity and handshake, then sends Finished. Shared secrets are derived into separate traffic keys, and application data uses authenticated symmetric encryption.
The certificate’s hostname, trust chain and validity must be checked. Optional client authentication adds client credentials. Older textbook TLS/SSL handshakes can use different message ordering and RSA key transport; do not mix those with this TLS 1.3 diagram.
items.final: Negotiate, authenticate server, derive keys and exchange encrypted authenticated data.

items.title: Static versus dynamic analysis
items.body: Static analysis examines a suspicious file without running it: inspect hashes, strings, metadata, imports and code structure. It is safer to begin with but obfuscation can hide behavior. Dynamic analysis runs the file in a controlled isolated environment and observes process, filesystem, registry and network behavior. It can reveal runtime actions but may miss delayed or environment-aware behavior. Use snapshots, restricted networking and an appropriately isolated lab; never run an unknown file on a working machine merely to inspect it.
items.final: Static inspects without execution; dynamic observes behavior during isolated execution.

items.title: How DNSSEC counters cache poisoning
items.body:
A signed zone publishes signatures over record sets. A validating resolver checks the record signature using the zone DNSKEY and validates the delegation chain through DS/DNSKEY relationships to a configured trust anchor. A forged record cannot normally produce a valid signature, so a bogus signed answer is rejected rather than accepted into cache.
The diagram shows the chain of trust and the validation decision. DNSSEC supplies data-origin authentication and integrity, including authenticated denial for properly signed negative answers; it does not encrypt DNS traffic or guarantee that an unsigned domain is secure. It also does not fix a compromised legitimate signing key or malicious authorized zone content.
items.final: Validate signed DNS data through a trust chain; reject bogus signatures.

items.title: HTTPS/TLS session for data transfer
items.body:
HTTPS carries HTTP inside an authenticated encrypted TLS channel. Resolve and connect to the intended hostname, negotiate TLS, validate the server’s certificate and handshake proof, derive session traffic keys, and then exchange HTTP requests/responses protected by authenticated encryption. The server typically proves possession of a private authentication key; bulk data uses symmetric session keys.
The TLS diagram illustrates version 1.3. HTTPS protects the connection to the validated hostname; it does not guarantee that a site’s content or business is honest, nor protect data after a compromised endpoint decrypts it.
items.final: HTTP over a validated TLS connection uses symmetric authenticated encryption for data.

items.title: Session hijacking and mitigations
items.body:
An attacker impersonates a logged-in user by obtaining or fixing an authenticated session identifier. Possible causes include exposed cookies, XSS, insecure transport, predictable tokens or failure to rotate an identifier after login.
Use HTTPS throughout; high-entropy tokens; Secure, HttpOnly and appropriate SameSite cookies; rotation after authentication/privilege changes; idle and absolute expiry; server-side invalidation on logout; XSS prevention and reauthentication for sensitive actions. CSRF protection prevents a different class of unauthorized action and remains useful, but is not a substitute for protecting session tokens.
items.final: Protect, rotate, expire and revoke unpredictable session identifiers.

items.title: URL obfuscation example
items.body:
URL obfuscation makes a destination look like a trusted site through misleading text, lookalike hostnames, encoding or user-info syntax. Safe illustrative example: https://trusted.example@evil.example/login has hostname evil.example; trusted.example is user-info before @. Another example is trusted.example.evil.example, which is under evil.example, not trusted.example. All example domains are reserved for documentation.
Inspect the actual parsed hostname, use trusted bookmarks and password-manager origin matching, and avoid relying on link display text alone. HTTPS to the wrong hostname still encrypts a connection to that wrong hostname.
items.final: Misleading URL text hides the actual destination; inspect the true hostname.

items.title: SQL injection and prevention
items.body:
SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into SQL and changes its structure. In a toy login query built as SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='<input>', an input containing a quote and SQL syntax can change the predicate rather than remain a name value. This illustrates the flaw without targeting a service.
Use a parameterized query such as SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=? and bind the value separately. The database then treats the value as data, not executable SQL. Use allowlists for identifiers that cannot be parameters, least-privilege database accounts and safe error handling. Store passwords with an appropriate password hash and verify them correctly; query safety does not replace password security.
items.final: Separate SQL code from values with bound parameters; never concatenate untrusted input.
